name: Caladbolg
powers: Legendary sword of Cú Chulainn, capable of slicing the head off a boar with a single stroke.
description: Caladbolg, the great sword of Irish legend, is carried in the Ulster Cycle by Fergus mac Róich, the strong-armed former king of Ulster, and in some traditions it is also the blade of Cú Chulainn, who is said to have wielded it in the great single combat against his foster-brother Ferdiad in the Táin Bó Cúailnge. Its name, often translated 'hard lightning' or 'hard cleft', describes a sword of fearsome cutting power. The word is the Irish cognate of the British Caledfwlch, the sword of Arthur better known as Excalibur, which makes Caladbolg the Irish link in the family of the great legendary blades of the Celtic world. In the tale of the Feast of Bricriu the sword is counted among the marvels tested by the heroes. No historical sword bearing the name survives, so its power is entirely in the literature, and it stands for the violent, glamorous world of the sagas.

name: Excalibur
powers: Blade that cut through any armor; scabbard protected the wearer from wounding.
description: The great sword of King Arthur, given to him by the Lady of the Lake after he broke his first blade, and returned to her waters by Sir Bedivere when Arthur died at Camlann. In Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur (1485) the scabbard, not the blade, is the true treasure, since it protects the wearer from wounding in battle. The name, from the Latin Caliburnus and the Welsh Caledfwlch, also attaches in later romance to the sword Arthur drew from the stone, though the oldest sources keep the two blades separate. The weapon already appears in Welsh tradition in Culhwch ac Olwen, where Arthur's sword Caledfwlch is named among his possessions. Its giving and return make it a gift of the Otherworld that cannot be kept by mortal hands, a pattern echoed across Celtic legend. Excalibur has become the archetypal magic sword of modern fantasy, carried into films, games and retellings of the Arthurian cycle.

name: Claíomh Mór
powers: Said to bite through any armor or shield.
description: Claíomh Mór, 'the great sword' of Irish tradition, is one of the four treasures the Tuatha Dé Danann carried with them when they came to Ireland, and later lore links it to Nuada Airgetlám, king of the Tuatha Dé Danann. In the Lebor Gabála Érenn the sword of Nuada is said to be irresistible once drawn from its sheath, and it is listed beside the spear of Lugh, the cauldron of the Dagda and the stone of Fal. The name is close to, and often confused with, Claíomh Solais, the sword of light, a term that later folklore attached to the magic weapons of heroes and even to a buried golden sword that would rise against the invader. Some regional retellings describe the blade as drawing light from the Otherworld so that it blazed like a torch in battle. The sword remains a staple of Irish storytelling and has been invoked in poetry, ballad and political symbolism.

name: Dyrnwyn
powers: Burst into flame when drawn by a worthy man; burned the unworthy bearer.
description: Dyrnwyn, meaning 'white-hilt', is the sword of Rhydderch Hael, the Generous, one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain listed in medieval Welsh texts. If anyone but Rhydderch himself drew the blade from its scabbard it burst into flame from its cross-guard to its point, burning the unworthy bearer until it was sheathed again. Rhydderch, famed as one of the Three Generous Men of Britain, refused no one who asked to borrow the sword, but every borrower quickly handed it back once its fiery property was revealed. The treasure list survives in a group of Welsh manuscripts, and the earliest versions record only the names of the treasures without explanation. The sword is sometimes said to have been drawn by a noble warrior who alone could wield it without harm, though the tradition records nothing more of its fate. Dyrnwyn belongs to the same family of test-weapons as many Celtic blades, punishing the unfit and rewarding the worthy.
source: Medieval Welsh list of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain

name: Gáe Assail
powers: Unstoppable spear of the champion of the Tuatha Dé Danann.
description: Gáe Assail, the great spear of Lugh, is one of the four treasures the Tuatha Dé Danann brought to Ireland, and Lugh carried it into battle at the Second Battle of Mag Tuired against the Fomorians. The Lebor Gabála Érenn and Cath Maige Tuired describe it as a weapon of such force that no warrior could withstand it, and Lugh, who arrives at the battle as champion of the Tuatha Dé Danann, uses it in the rout of the Fomorian host. Its name, sometimes written Gáe Assal, links it to the Otherworld gift-bearers of Irish tradition, and later manuscripts count it among the possessions the god brought from across the sea. In some retellings the spear is said to thirst so strongly for battle that it had to be kept in a vessel of soporific herbs to calm it, a detail that echoes the restless weapons of Celtic legend. It survives today as a symbol of Lugh's kingship and of the ancient Irish world of craft and war.

name: The Green Knight's Axe
powers: Weapon of the beheading challenge at Camelot.
description: The enormous green-steel axe carried by the Green Knight into King Arthur's hall at Camelot on New Year's Eve in the fourteenth-century alliterative poem Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. The weapon, described as an unwieldy blade of enormous size, is the instrument of the beheading game: Gawain strikes off the Knight's head with it, and the Knight calmly picks up the severed head, which reminds Gawain to meet him at the Green Chapel in a year and a day. The axe thus becomes the token of the exchange-of-blows bargain that drives the poem's testing of Gawain's honour. When Gawain flinches at the first swing of the return blow, the Knight taunts him with the very blade Gawain had used. The axe is sometimes read as a symbol of the winter god or the old year passing, its green steel binding the natural and chivalric worlds. It remains one of the most memorable props in medieval English literature.
source: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (fourteenth century)

name: Tara Brooch
material: Silver-gilt, gold filigree, amber and glass
description: The Tara Brooch, a masterpiece of early medieval Irish metalwork, is a silver-gilt annular brooch decorated with gold filigree panels, amber studs and coloured glass, made in Ireland around the eighth century AD. It was found in 1850 on the beach near Bettystown, County Meath, and was given the name 'Tara' by its first owner to exploit the royal associations of the Hill of Tara for sale. The brooch is one of the finest surviving examples of Insular art, its interlacing animal and geometric patterns echoing the illuminated manuscripts of the same period, and it survives with its original chain and pin intact, a rarity for its age. Such brooches were status symbols worn at the shoulder to fasten a cloak, the standard dress-fastener of the early medieval Irish elite. It is now displayed in the National Museum of Ireland in Dublin, where it remains one of the most admired objects of Celtic jewellery in the world.

name: Great Torc of Snettisham
description: The Great Torc of Snettisham is a large neck-ring of two interlocking gold-alloy tubes with ornate buffer terminals, made in eastern England around 75 BC and worn by a high-status Iron Age Briton. It was found in 1950 in the famous Snettisham hoard excavations in Norfolk, where ploughing repeatedly revealed pits packed with torcs, bracelets and coins. The torc was cast by a lost-wax process in a gold-silver-copper alloy that gives it a pale, silvery gleam, and its twisted bodies and polished terminals are masterpieces of Celtic metalwork. Torcs signalled rank and wealth across the Celtic world, worn by warriors, chieftains and sometimes gods, and classical writers record that the Gauls wore gold neck-rings in battle. The Great Torc is dated by the coins found with it and is usually displayed with the slightly larger Snettisham Great Torc of the same hoard. It forms the centrepiece of the British Museum's Iron Age Celtic collection.

name: Claddagh Ring
description: The Claddagh ring, a gold or silver finger-ring shaped as two hands clasping a crowned heart, has been made in Galway since the seventeenth century and is named after the old fishing village of Claddagh beside the city. The design descends from the medieval 'fede' ring, whose clasped hands stood for faith and betrothal, with the heart and crown added locally. The best-known origin story tells of Richard Joyce, a Galway goldsmith who was captured by Algerian pirates in the late seventeenth century and sold into slavery in North Africa, where he supposedly made the ring before returning home; the tale is recorded in James Hardiman's 1820 History of Galway, though its details cannot be fully verified. The oldest surviving Claddagh ring, dated to about 1700 and stamped with Joyce's mark, is held by Galway City Museum. The ring is still a living custom, passed down from mother to daughter and worn in different positions to show whether the wearer is single or betrothed.

name: Prydwen
powers: Arthur's vessel for voyages to the Otherworld stronghold of Annwn.
description: Prydwen, in Welsh tradition, is the name of King Arthur's ship, the vessel in which he sails on expeditions into the Otherworld. In Culhwch ac Olwen Arthur rides in Prydwen, and in the poem Preiddeu Annwn, the Spoils of Annwn, he sails in the ship with a chosen company to raid the cauldron of the Otherworld fortress of Annwn. The name, which some scholars connect with a word meaning 'beautiful form', is also given to Arthur's shield in some texts, so that a single word came to serve for both protection on land and passage by sea. The voyage to Annwn belongs to the oldest stratum of Arthurian legend, before the continental romances of the court and the Grail. Prydwen's journey places Arthur among the voyagers of Celtic tradition who cross the sea to the lands of the dead, a motif shared with the Irish immrama, or voyage-tales.

name: Mantle of Tegau Eurfron
powers: Fitted only a wife faithful to her husband; exposed unfaithful wives.
description: Tegau Eurfron's mantle, the Mantle of Tegau Gold-Breast, is one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain listed in medieval Welsh tradition. The garment would fit only a woman who had been faithful to her husband; a wife who had broken her vows could not wear it, and it would not cover her, revealing the truth of her conduct to the court. Tegau herself, the wife of Caradog, is praised in the Welsh triads as one of the three faithful wives of Britain, and the mantle is the token of her chastity. The object belongs to a family of chastity-testing garments found across medieval Europe, from the Arthurian mantel mal taillé to the test-mantles of later romance. Like the other treasures, the mantle is described in the later manuscript lists with explanatory notes. The Welsh tale survives as a parable of marriage, honesty and the public testing of private virtue.
source: Medieval Welsh list of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain

name: Arthur's Mantle
powers: Made the wearer invisible while still allowing them to see everything around them.
description: Arthur's mantle, Llen Arthur, is one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain in medieval Welsh tradition. Whoever wore the cloak became invisible, yet could still see everything about him, a power that made it a garment of spies and guardians. The treasure list, which survives in several Welsh manuscripts from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, records the object among the possessions of the old heroes of British legend, and one version places the mantle 'in Cornwall'. The cloak belongs to the Welsh Arthur of marvel and quest, distinct from the later continental king of Malory and the French romances. Its power of selective invisibility, hiding the wearer while leaving his sight intact, is echoed in later folklore and fantasy. Unlike Arthur's sword and ship, the mantle appears nowhere outside the Welsh treasure catalogue, and it remains one of the more mysterious items in the list.
source: Medieval Welsh list of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain

name: Selkie's Seal-Skin
powers: Lets the selkie shed human form and return to the sea when put back on.
description: The seal-skin of the selkie is the central object of the seal-people tales of Scotland, Ireland and the northern isles, a pelt that lets its wearer take human form on land. A selkie who wishes to return to the sea must put the skin back on, so a human who steals and hides the skin can hold a selkie bride or husband captive, and the marriage lasts only until the skin is found and returned. The motif drives the classic selkie-bride stories, from the Faroese tale of Kópakonan to the Hebridean, Orcadian and Icelandic variants collected by folklorists, in which the wife grieves by the shore until a child or a neighbour reveals the hiding-place. The stolen skin gives the tale its haunting shape: love bought by captivity, and the sea always calling. The skin is sometimes said to be hidden in a chest or under a roof beam, and its discovery is always the turning point. In modern retellings the seal-skin has become a symbol of identity, longing and the cost of belonging to two worlds.

name: Silver Branch of Emain
powers: Its music lulled listeners and summoned heroes to the Otherworld.
description: The silver branch of Emain is the singing apple-branch carried by a woman of the Otherworld who visits the hero Bran mac Febail in the medieval Irish tale Immram Brain, the Voyage of Bran. The branch bears silver apples and sweet blossoms, and its music lulls those who hear it to sleep while the branch itself sings of the delights of the Land of Women across the sea. When Bran refuses to part with the branch and follows its bearer, he begins the famous voyage that carries him and his company from island to wonder-filled island. Messengers of the Irish Otherworld are traditionally shown bearing such singing branches of apple, a token of the supernatural world's beauty and its power to summon mortals away. The branch's music, which opens the mind to the otherworld, marks it as one of the most evocative of Irish wonder-objects. It later found its way into the poetry of W.B. Yeats, who drew on the image of the silver and golden bough.

name: Cormac's Cup
powers: Shattered at a spoken lie and restored itself when truth was told.
description: The cup of Cormac mac Airt appears in Echtra Cormaic, the Adventure of Cormac, a medieval Irish tale in which a warrior who is really Manannán mac Lir gives the high king a golden cup in exchange for his wife and daughter. The cup is a cup of truth: if three lies are spoken over it, it breaks into pieces, and if three truths are told it is made whole again, so that Cormac uses it to test the words of his court. In the end Cormac learns that his wife and daughter have been carried to the Otherworld, and the cup is restored to him along with the lesson that no man can hold the truth's secrets without giving up what he loves. The tale, recorded in the Book of Ballymote and related manuscripts, belongs to the tradition of moral test-objects in Irish wonder literature. The cup is sometimes called the cup of truth, and its shattering and mending remain its best-known feature.
source: Echtra Cormaic (The Adventure of Cormac mac Airt)

name: Cauldron of Rebirth
powers: Restored slain warriors to life, though the revived could not speak.
description: Pair Dadeni, the Cauldron of Rebirth, appears in the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, the story of Branwen daughter of Llŷr, where it is given to Bran the Blessed by a giant couple, Llassar Llaes Gyfnewid and his wife, who have carried it out of Ireland. Warriors slain in battle and cast into the cauldron are restored to life, though the revived come back unable to speak. When Bran invades Ireland to avenge the insult to Branwen, the cauldron is used to raise the enemy dead again and again, until Efnysien, the family's half-brother, destroys it by throwing himself into it and bursting it apart. The cauldron thus carries both the power of rebirth and the need for its own sacrifice. Scholars connect it with the Irish cauldrons of plenty and with the later Grail legends. Its story remains among the strangest and most discussed episodes of the Mabinogion.

name: Cauldron of the Dagda
powers: No company ever went away from it unsatisfied.
description: Coire an Dagda, the cauldron of the Dagda, is one of the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann carried into Ireland and described in the Lebor Gabála Érenn. The cauldron of plenty is said to be so generous that no company ever left it unsatisfied, feeding any number of people from its unfailing depths. It is named beside the spear of Lugh, the sword of Nuada and the stone of Fal as one of the great wonder-gifts of the Old Gods, and the four treasures together symbolise the powers of kingship, war and plenty that the Tuatha Dé Danann brought to the island. In the later tradition of the Cath Maige Tuired the Dagda himself is a god of fertility and abundance, and his cauldron matches his appetite and generosity. The cauldron is sometimes linked to the Irish motif of the endless vessel that feeds all comers, a theme found across Celtic folklore. It remains the archetype of the cauldron of abundance in Irish myth.
source: Lebor Gabála Érenn; four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann

name: Lia Fáil
powers: Cried out beneath the rightful king of Ireland when he stood on it.
description: Lia Fáil, the Stone of Destiny, stands on the hill of Tara and is one of the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann in Irish tradition. In the Lebor Gabála Érenn it is counted among the treasures carried into Ireland, and later tales say the stone cried out beneath the rightful king when he stood or stepped on it, so that the whole assembly heard its voice. The best-known account is in Baile in Scáil, where the stone roars under the high king Conn of the Hundred Battles and reveals the line of kings who will follow him. Medieval writers and antiquaries long claimed that the Irish stone was the same as the Stone of Scone used in the coronation of the kings of Scotland, a belief still attached to the Lia Fáil by visitors to Tara. The present standing stone on the hill is a weathered monolith, and its identification with the legendary stone is itself a matter of debate. It remains the most potent symbol of Irish kingship.
source: Lebor Gabála Érenn; Baile in Scáil

name: Ardagh Chalice
material: Silver, bronze, gold filigree, glass and enamel
description: The Ardagh Chalice is a two-handled silver cup made in Ireland in the eighth century AD and found in 1868, together with a hoard of other church metalwork and a bronze pin, inside a ring-fort at Ardagh in County Limerick. The vessel is built of silver with a bronze core, and its decoration of gold filigree, glass studs and enamel panels, executed in the interlacing animal style of Insular art, ranks it among the greatest treasures of early medieval Europe. It was probably made for use at Mass in a wealthy monastery, and it shares its technical brilliance with the contemporary Derrynaflan Chalice and the illuminated gospel manuscripts of the same age. The hoard in which it was found had been concealed in a stone-lined hollow beneath the fort, apparently during a time of danger. The chalice is displayed in the National Museum of Ireland in Dublin, where it is a centrepiece of the medieval collection and a national icon.

name: The Grail of Peredur
description: The dish or salver carried in the mysterious procession at the castle in the medieval Welsh romance Peredur ab Efrawg is the Welsh cousin of the Holy Grail. In the romance, Peredur, staying at a strange castle, watches a procession in which a youth carries a spear with blood dripping from its tip, followed by a woman bearing a salver on which lies a severed head. Peredur does not ask about what he has seen, and for his silence he is cursed; only later does he learn that the head was that of his cousin, slain in vengeance, and that the vision was linked with the wounding of the Grail king. Unlike the French Grail romances of Chrétien de Troyes, the Welsh text centres on the bleeding head and the dish rather than a chalice, preserving a distinct Celtic strand of the legend. The tale survives in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest. The object is legendary and unattested, but Peredur's procession remains one of the most debated scenes in Arthurian literature.

name: Nanteos Cup
description: The Nanteos Cup is a small, badly damaged wooden bowl, a late medieval mazer of wych elm, held for many years at Nanteos mansion near Aberystwyth in Ceredigion and kept today by the descendants of the Powell family. From at least the late nineteenth century it was treated as a healing cup: sick people borrowed it, leaving a valuable pledge, and drank from it in the hope of a cure, and its jagged edge was blamed on pilgrims who bit or scraped off pieces as relics. Some traditions said the bowl was made from a piece of the True Cross, and after 1905, when a visitor published Sought and Found, it was proclaimed one of at least two hundred European candidates for the Holy Grail. Folklorists have shown that there is no credible reference to the cup before about 1836, and no connection with the Grail before 1905, with one legend holding that monks carried it from Glastonbury to Strata Florida during the Dissolution of the Monasteries. The cup is now preserved at the National Library of Wales, a living relic of Welsh folklore.

name: Ceridwen's Cauldron
powers: Brewed the Awen, the drops of inspiration and knowledge, for a year and a day.
description: Ceridwen's cauldron belongs to the medieval Ystoria Taliesin, the Tale of Taliesin, in which the enchantress Ceridwen, a figure of wisdom and magic, brews a potion of inspiration and knowledge in a great cauldron for her son Afagddu. The brew must simmer for a year and a day, and the three drops of its divine inspiration, the Awen, fall instead on the boy Gwion, who guards the pot and swallows them, gaining all its wisdom at a stroke. Ceridwen pursues Gwion through a series of transformations, each side changing shape until she swallows him as a grain of wheat, and in time bears the child who becomes the poet Taliesin. The cauldron thus stands at the origin of the Welsh bardic tradition, the source of the Awen that inspires poets and seers. It is sometimes linked by scholars to the cauldrons of rebirth and plenty in Celtic myth. The object is wholly legendary, known only from the medieval tale and its retellings.

name: Green Knight's Holly Branch
description: The holly branch carried by the Green Knight in the opening scenes of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight marks him as a figure of the winter season when he rides into Arthur's hall on New Year's Eve. The poem says the knight carried no shield or spear, only a holly bough in one hand and the great axe in the other, the evergreen symbol of the old year's endurance. He holds the branch in the same hand that grips the axe as he delivers his challenge, so that the two objects together present him as a green man of the turning year. Some readers see the holly as a sign of peace, since it was the emblem used in medieval Christmas observances, while others read it as the badge of a wild, pre-Christian power that intrudes on the court. In the poem's seasonal frame the branch connects the challenge to the cycle of death and renewal. It remains one of the most discussed details of the medieval masterpiece.
source: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight

name: The Round Table
powers: Seated all the knights of Arthur's court without quarrels over precedence.
description: The Round Table of King Arthur is the great council table at which, in Arthurian romance, no knight could claim a higher seat than another, ending the quarrels over precedence that divided the court. In Geoffrey of Monmouth's twelfth-century History of the Kings of Britain the table is only mentioned among Arthur's household furniture, but later romance writers made it the heart of the court and the scene of the knights' vows. In some versions, notably the prose romances, the table is devised by Merlin, and the perilous seat at it is reserved for the knight who will win the Grail, with disaster striking any unworthy claimant. A great painted table said to be Arthur's hangs in the Great Hall of Winchester Castle, made in the thirteenth century and repainted in Tudor times. The table came to symbolise the ideal of equal fellowship among knights, an image that passed into modern politics and culture. It remains one of the defining symbols of the Arthurian world.
source: Geoffrey of Monmouth; Arthurian romance; Winchester table

name: The Singing Harp
powers: Sang on its own and cried out for its master, waking the giant.
description: The singing harp of the giant in the English fairy tale Jack and the Beanstalk is one of the three treasures Jack steals on his second visit to the giant's castle in the clouds, beside the bag of gold and the hen that lays golden eggs. The harp plays by itself, and as Jack flees down the beanstalk it calls out 'Master! Master!', waking the giant and setting the pursuit in motion. When Jack reaches the ground he chops the beanstalk down and the giant falls to his death, so the harp's voice is the object that turns the theft into the tale's climax. The story, first printed in the eighteenth century and popularised in chapbooks and pantomime, makes the harp a magic object of the fairy-tale kind, able to sing and to act on its own will. The harp, the hen and the gold recall the classic triad of fairy-tale treasures. Its self-playing music marks it as one of the earliest and most famous talking objects in English folklore.
source: Jack and the Beanstalk (English fairy tale)
